hero.title: NestJS + Nuxt 4
hero.subtitle:
Production-ready starting point for full-stack applications.
Deploy in minutes, scale to production.

showcase.title: What it's built on
showcase.lead: Mature tools with large communities and active releases only. No experimental dependencies you'll have to rip out six months from now.
showcase.optionalNote: Optional modules: enabled by choice when you create a project. The base template runs without them.

transparency.title: Transparency
transparency.desc: No magic. Every decision is explained and obvious from the code.

idiomatic.title: Idiomatic
idiomatic.desc: Follow NestJS and Nuxt conventions, don't reinvent the wheel.

production.title: Production-ready
production.desc: Docker, env validation, error handling — from day one.

starter.title: Start for your ideas
starter.desc: A ready foundation — clone it and build your product instead of spending weeks on boilerplate.

fit.title: Who it's for — and who it isn't
fit.lead: An honest breakdown instead of a feature list. The template commits you to a separate API server and an SSR frontend — a win where that architecture is needed, dead weight where it isn't.

summary.title: In short
for: build a new user account area from scratch
a private area alongside the public one
an API of your own — for web, a mobile app or integrations
a BFF in front of existing services: aggregate calls and keep secrets out of the frontend
SSR for fast first paint and SEO
build alongside an AI assistant: a proven foundation and detailed docs it picks up from the start
against: the site has no account area or login
content lives in files or a headless CMS
static files on a CDN are enough
you deploy to serverless or the edge
you need a plain proxy to an existing API, with no aggregation or logic of your own

saas.name: SaaS with a user account area
saas.why: Exactly what the template was built for: sign-up, login, sessions, roles, a public side and a protected one. The auth-session branch covers authentication, leaving you the domain logic.

admin.name: Admin panel, CRM, internal dashboard
admin.why: Lots of forms, tables and access rules. NestJS ships DTO validation and guards; Nuxt gives file-based routing and middleware to gate pages. SSR is a bonus here — the panel opens fast even on a slow laptop.

landing.name: Landing or promo page
landing.why: A separate API server, a database and Docker plumbing for the sake of one contact form means weeks of upkeep for nothing — plus two running processes instead of static files on a CDN.
landing.alt: Astro, or Nuxt in static mode with a hosted form service.

mobileBackend.name: Backend for a mobile app
mobileBackend.why: The NestJS side stands on its own: REST with a Swagger schema, validation, errors in a single shape. Keep the frontend as a content admin panel or drop it entirely — the backend doesn't change either way.

contentSite.name: Blog, docs, content site
contentSite.why: Content belongs in files or a headless CMS, not in tables you design yourself. A NestJS backend does nothing here beyond serving text.
contentSite.alt: Astro, VitePress or Nuxt Content — these very docs run on VitePress.

mvp.name: Startup MVP
mvp.why: The first two weeks usually go to plumbing: configs, linters, auth, Docker, deployment. That's already here and documented, so you can test the hypothesis instead of configuring a build.

microservices.name: Microservice system
microservices.why: A pnpm workspaces monorepo handles several services well, and NestJS supports transports beyond HTTP. But the template brings no service discovery, no queues and no tracing — that's on you to build.
microservices.alt: Starting from this monorepo is reasonable; budget for the infrastructure work.

serverless.name: Serverless and edge functions
serverless.why: NestJS builds a DI container at startup, which costs real hundreds of milliseconds on a cold start. A long-lived PostgreSQL connection pool fits that model poorly too.
serverless.alt: Hono or Nuxt's Nitro routes, with an HTTP-protocol database driver.

learning.name: Learning full-stack TypeScript
learning.why: The template's rule is no magic: every non-obvious decision has a comment in the code and a page in the docs. You can see how SSR, cookie sessions, guards and migrations connect — in real code, not a todo-app tutorial.

highLoad.name: High traffic from day one
highLoad.why: The architecture scales horizontally just fine: a stateless API with sessions in the database. But there's no cache, no rate limiting, no queues and no metrics — under serious expected load you'll need to add those deliberately.
highLoad.alt: Plan Redis, a queue and monitoring before launch, not after.

legacy.name: A frontend for existing services
legacy.why: Depends on what Nest does. If it aggregates calls across several services, keeps secrets out of the frontend and adds access rules of its own, that's a BFF and the template works as intended. If it forwards requests one-to-one, the extra process doesn't pay for itself.
legacy.alt: For plain proxying — Nuxt's Nitro routes, no separate backend.

internalTools.name: Internal company tools
internalTools.why: Dashboards, export services, support panels. Traffic is predictable, SEO doesn't matter, and what does matter — development speed and understandable auth — is already covered.

fit.note: These verdicts aren't verdicts on you: almost every "pick something else" case is buildable on this template. They judge whether the complexity it brings pays for itself.

auth.title: Authentication
auth.lead: The base template ships without authentication — if you want to build your own, there is nothing to rip out. Ready-made auth comes as a separate option layered on top of the base.

base.label: base template
base.title: Without auth
base.desc: A clean starting point: Nest, Nuxt and shared types. Plug in your provider or write a scheme that fits your requirements.

layer.label: option
layer.title: With auth
layer.desc: Fully working authentication on top of the base option. Do not spend weeks on what is already written and battle-tested.

auth.pointsTitle: What the option with auth includes

tokens.title: JWT access + refresh.
tokens.desc: Access lives 15 minutes and is verified without hitting the store, refresh lives 7 days and can be revoked instantly.

cookies.title: httpOnly cookies.
cookies.desc: Tokens are unreachable from JavaScript, SameSite=strict closes CSRF. Nothing is kept in localStorage.

rotation.title: Rotation and reuse detection.
rotation.desc: Every refresh issues a new token. Reusing an old one counts as theft — the session chain is cut off.

sessions.title: Server-side sessions.
sessions.desc: A list of active devices, sign-out on a specific one, and an instant sign-out everywhere on password change.

roles.title: Roles and guards.
roles.desc: user and admin, the @Public() and @Roles() decorators, route protection on the backend and middleware on the frontend.

ssr.title: Works with SSR.
ssr.desc: Silent refresh before the page renders: F5 with an expired token neither kicks you to the login page nor causes a hydration mismatch.

providers.title: Can be extended.
providers.desc: OAuth, OIDC or an external provider can be added on top — the current scheme does not stand in the way and needs no rewrite.

auth.note: The scheme is JWT access + refresh with server-side rotation — the same approach most web apps with a separate API use. The alternatives and the reasoning behind the choice are covered

main.label: Base
main.desc: Starting point without a database. Users CRUD is stored in-memory.

postgresPrisma.label: PostgreSQL
postgresPrisma.desc: Adds PostgreSQL and Prisma 7 on top of the Auth variant.

auth.label: Auth
auth.desc: The perfect starting point for dashboards and admin panels. JWT authentication on top of the base variant: email + password, httpOnly cookies, sessions in process memory.
